questions.question_text: Financial statements provide information on

options.C: profits or losses incurred by the company

questions.explanation: Financial statements (Balance Sheet, P&L, Cash Flow) provide comprehensive information: Balance Sheet shows assets and liabilities at a point in time; P&L shows profits/losses over a period; Cash Flow shows cash movements. Together they provide complete financial picture.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following options is most likely correct?
I. Sole-proprietorship business is owned by more than one person
II. The liability of the shareholders is limited upto unpaid amount on their shares.
III. The liability of the sole proprietor is unlimited.
IV. Partners have limited liability.
questions.explanation: II is correct: Shareholders in a Limited Company have limited liability up to unpaid amount on shares. III is correct: Sole proprietor has unlimited liability - personal assets can be used to pay business debts. I is wrong (sole proprietorship owned by 1 person). IV is wrong (partners typically have unlimited liability unless LLP).

questions.question_text: Creditors use the accounting information to check the ______________ of the business.
questions.explanation: Creditors (suppliers/lenders) use accounting information to assess liquidity - the ability to pay short-term obligations. They check current ratio, cash flow, and working capital to determine if the business can repay debts on time.

questions.question_text: Credit sales refers to

options.A: Both delivery of goods and collection of money at a future date
options.B: Amount is collected today and delivery will be effected at a future date
options.C: Both delivery of goods and collection of money happens today.
options.D: Goods sold today for which payment will be collected at a future date

questions.explanation: Credit sales means goods are delivered/sold today, but payment will be collected at a future date. This creates Accounts Receivable (debtor) - an asset representing the right to receive payment later.

questions.question_text: Ledger is a

options.C: record of cash and bank transactions
options.D: Summarised record of transactions that shows the net balance of each account

questions.explanation: Ledger is the book of final entry where transactions are classified by account. It shows the net balance (debit or credit) of each account after all transactions. It's a summarized record, not just a list or statement.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of real account?
Harish and Co. paid rent for its office Rs.5000 in cash. How would this transaction be recorded using double entry system of bookkeeping in the books of Harish and Co.?

options.A: Cash account will be debited and rent expense will be credited by Rs.5000
options.B: Office expenses will be debited and rent expense will be credited by Rs.5000
options.C: Harish and Co. will be debited and cash will be credited by Rs.5000
options.D: Rent expense will be debited and cash account will be credited by Rs.5000

questions.explanation: For Nominal Accounts (expenses): Debit all expenses and losses. Rent expense increases (Debit). Cash (Real Account) goes out - Credit. Entry: Dr. Rent Expense 5,000, Cr. Cash 5,000.

questions.question_text: On 1st March 2024, Savita and company took loan from SBI Rs.1,00,000 payable in two years at interest of 8%. The journal entry to record the same on 1st March 2024 will be

options.A: Cash and bank account debit Rs. 1,00,000; Interest account credit Rs. 1,00,000
options.B: SBI account debit Rs. 1,00,000; cash and bank account credit Rs. 1,00,000
options.C: Loan account debit Rs. 1,00,000; Interest account credit Rs. 1,00,000
options.D: Cash and bank account debit Rs. 1,00,000; Loan account credit Rs. 1,00,000

questions.explanation: When taking a loan: Cash (asset) increases - Debit; Loan (liability) increases - Credit. Entry: Dr. Cash and Bank Account 1,00,000, Cr. Loan Account 1,00,000. Interest is not recorded until it accrues.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the correct?
questions.explanation: The Accounting Equation is Assets = Liabilities + Equity. This is the fundamental equation that must always balance. All other rearrangements are mathematically equivalent but this is the standard form.

questions.question_text: Alex Co. purchased furniture of Rs.50,000 in cash. What will be the effect of this transaction on company's assets and liabilities?

options.A: Assets (furniture) will decrease by Rs.50,000 and Liabilities (creditor) will decrease by Rs.50,000
options.B: Assets (furniture) will increase by Rs.50,000 and Liabilities (creditor) will decrease by Rs.50,000
options.C: Assets (furniture) will decrease by Rs.50,000 and assets (cash) will increase by Rs.50,000
options.D: Assets (furniture) will increase by Rs.50,000 and assets (cash) will decrease by Rs.50,000

questions.explanation: Purchasing furniture for cash: Furniture (asset) increases (+50,000) and Cash (asset) decreases (-50,000). Net change in assets = 0. No change in liabilities. This is an exchange of one asset for another.

questions.question_text: ABC Ltd. was formed with a capital of Rs.100,000. What will be the effect of this transaction on company's accounting equation?

options.A: Increase in cash and decrease in capital
options.B: Increase in cash and decrease in liabilities
options.C: Decrease in cash and decrease in liabilities
options.D: Increase in cash and increase in capital

questions.question_text: A firm has assets of Rs. 200,000 and liabilities of Rs.80,000 at the year end. What is the total amount of equity at the year end?
questions.explanation: Using Accounting Equation: Equity = Assets - Liabilities = 200,000 - 80,000 = 120,000. Equity represents the residual interest in assets after deducting all liabilities.

questions.question_text: In a business, if the total assets amount to ₹1800,000 and the total liabilities are ₹1300,000, what is the owner's equity?
questions.explanation: Equity = Assets - Liabilities = 1,800,000 - 1,300,000 = 500,000. Owner's equity is the residual interest after all liabilities are deducted from assets.

questions.question_text: If total revenues are ₹600,000 and total expenses are ₹400,000, what is the net income?
questions.explanation: Net Income = Revenue - Expenses = 600,000 - 400,000 = 200,000. This is the bottom line profit after all expenses are deducted from revenue.

questions.question_text: In accounting, real accounts are permanent and do not close at the end of the accounting period. Which one of the following is an example of a real account?
questions.explanation: Real Accounts are permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, equity) that carry balances forward. Tables (Furniture) is a tangible asset - a Real Account. Sales, Rent, and Salary are Nominal Accounts (temporary) that close to P&L.

questions.question_text: When furniture worth ₹5,00,000 is purchased and paid for in cash, which account should be debited?
questions.explanation: For Real Accounts: Debit what comes in. Furniture (asset) comes in, so Furniture Account is debited. Cash (asset) goes out, so Cash Account is credited. Entry: Dr. Furniture Account, Cr. Cash Account.

questions.question_text: In a transaction where a building worth ₹20,00,000 is purchased and paid for in cash, which account should be credited?
In the case of selling goods on credit to Mr. X, what is the correct double-entry system accounting entry for this transaction?
questions.explanation: For credit sales: Mr. X (Personal Account - Receiver/Debtor) - Debit; Sales (Nominal Account - Income) - Credit. Golden rule: Debit the Receiver, Credit the Giver. Here, Mr. X receives goods, Sales gives income.

questions.question_text: What is the correct entry to record the purchase of a machine for ₹2,00,000, paid for in cash?
questions.explanation: In accounting equation: Machine (asset) increases (+200,000) and Cash (asset) decreases (-200,000). Net change in assets = 0. This is an exchange of one asset for another.

questions.question_text: Goods sold for cash worth ₹50,000 must be recorded properly. What is the correct journal entry for this cash sales transaction?
When salaries are paid to employees, the cash account is reduced, and the salary expense account is increased. For a salary payment of ₹10 k, what is the correct journal entry to record the expense?
questions.explanation: For Nominal Accounts (expenses): Debit all expenses. Salary Expense increases (Debit); Cash (asset) decreases (Credit). Entry: Dr. Salary Expense +10k, Cr. Cash -10k.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about a sole proprietorship?

options.A: The owner is personally liable for business debts
options.B: Liability is limited to the business's assets

questions.explanation: In a sole proprietorship, the owner and business are the same entity legally. The owner has unlimited liability - personal assets can be used to pay business debts. This is a key characteristic distinguishing it from limited companies.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about a Limited Company?

options.A: The owner is personally liable for business debts
options.D: The liability of shareholders is limited to the unpaid value of the shares

questions.explanation: In a Limited Company, shareholders have limited liability - their liability is limited to the unpaid value of their shares. They are not personally liable for business debts beyond their investment. This distinguishes companies from sole proprietorships.

questions.question_text: Income statement provides information on

options.C: Profits or losses incurred by the company

questions.explanation: Income Statement (P&L) provides information on profits or losses - it shows revenue, expenses, and net income over a period. Assets and liabilities are shown in the Balance Sheet, not the Income Statement.

questions.question_text: Premier Ltd. follows the accounting period of 1st April to 31st March. The company opened a fixed deposit in bank on 1st April and deposited Rs. 50 lakhs at an interest rate of 12% per year for one year. The bank pays interest on 30th June and 31st December. The accounting entry on 31st March is:

options.B: Debit: Interest Accrued Rs. 1.5 Lakhs; Credit: Interest Income Rs. 1.5 lakhs
options.C: Debit: Interest Income Rs. 1.5 Lakhs; Credit: Interest Accrued Rs. 1.5 lakhs
options.D: Debit: Fixed Deposit Rs. 1.5 Lakhs; Credit: Interest Income Rs. 1.5 lakhs

questions.explanation: Interest earned but not received must be accrued. Deposit = 50 lakhs, Rate = 12%, Period = 1st Jan to 31st March (3 months). Interest = 50 × 12% × 3/12 = 1.5 lakhs. Entry: Dr. Interest Accrued (Asset), Cr. Interest Income (Revenue).

questions.question_text: Premier Ltd. took an insurance policy on 1st October 2023 and paid the insurance preimum of Rs. 120,000 for one year effective from 1st Oct 2023. Assuming the accountant debited the entire Rs. 120,000 as insurance expense on 1st Oct 2023, what adjustment entry needs to be entered to record the correct insurance expense for the year ended 31st March 2024 ?

options.A: Debit Insurance expense Rs.120,000; Credit cash and bank account Rs.120,000
options.B: Debit Prepaid Insurance Rs.120,000; Credit cash and bank account Rs.120,000
options.C: Debit Insurance expense Rs.60,000; Credit cash and bank account Rs.60,000
options.D: Debit Prepaid Insurance Rs.60,000; Credit insurance expense Rs.60,000

questions.question_text: Advance paid to the supplier is an example of
questions.explanation: Advance paid to supplier is a prepayment - it represents a future economic benefit (right to receive goods/services). It's an asset (similar to prepaid expenses) that will be converted to inventory/expense when goods are received.

questions.question_text: Salary expense for the month of March 2024 was paid on Arpil 10, 2024. The accountant failed to record the transaction on 31st March. What should be adjustment entry for the same on March 31, 2024?

options.A: Salary account debit; cash and bank account credit
options.B: Salary account credit; cash and bank account debit
options.C: Outstanding Salary account debit; cash and bank account credit
options.D: Salary account debit; outstanding salary account credit

questions.question_text: The company generated a sales of Rs. 100,000 for the year. The accountant estimated 2% of sales will be uncollectible. The accounting entry to record the same would be

options.A: Debit cash and bank Rs.98,000; Credit debtors Rs. 98,000
options.B: Debit bad debt (expense) Rs.2,000; Credit debtors Rs. 2,000
options.C: Debit bad debt (expense) Rs. 2,000; Credit provision for doubtful debt Rs. 2,000
options.D: Debit debtors Rs. 2,000; Credit provision for doubtful debt Rs. 2,000

questions.explanation: Provision for doubtful debts entry: Dr. Bad Debt Expense (increases expense), Cr. Provision for Doubtful Debts (contra-asset/liability). This creates a provision matching the expense with revenue, following Conservatism and Matching concepts. Estimated uncollectible = 100,000 × 2% = 2,000.

questions.question_text: Harish and Co. is a new trading firm engaged in buying and selling garments. During the year ended, the firm had sales of Rs. 6,00,000 and had closing inventory worth Rs.50,000. The firm sold goods at mark up of 20 per cent. What should be the cost of sales of the firm for the year?
questions.explanation: Mark up 20% means if cost = 100, selling price = 120. Sales = 600,000. Cost = 600,000 / 1.20 = 500,000. Alternatively: If markup is 20% on cost, then sales = 120% of cost. Cost = 600,000 / 1.20 = 500,000.

questions.question_text: Ram and Sons paid Rs. 200,000 to its suppliers for purchasing goods. This will be reported as
questions.explanation: Payment to suppliers for purchasing goods is an operating activity - it relates to principal revenue-generating activities (purchasing inventory for resale). Operating activities include cash from customers, payments to suppliers, salaries, and taxes paid.

questions.question_text: Gamma Co. purchased equipment worth Rs. 100,000. They paid transportation charges of Rs. 20,000. The installation expenses pad to the technician was Rs. 2000. What is the amount that will be reflected under cash flow from investing activity in the cash flow statement?
A company repaid loan Rs. 100,000 during the year. This be shown as --------
questions.explanation: Loan repayment is a financing activity - it involves changes in borrowings. Financing activities include taking/repaying loans, issue of shares, and dividends paid. Repayment reduces debt, appearing as cash outflow under financing.

questions.question_text: Ms. Gita, Mita and Nita contributed Rs. 6 lakh each and started a partnership to offer customised interior for HNI clients. They shared profit or loss equally. At the end of three years, their friend Rita joined the firm and contributed Rs. 2 lakhs for a one-fourth share in the firm. The partners decided to revalue their business and estimated the goodwill value to be 5 times the last 3 years average profit. The average profit for the last 3 years was Rs. 300,000. What is the amount of goodwill of the firm when new partner joined the firm and the new profit sharing ratio?

options.A: Rs. 3,00,000 and the new profit sharing ratio is 33.33:16.67:16.67:33.33
options.B: Rs. 6,00,000 and the new profit sharing ratio is 33.33:16.67:16.67:33.33
options.C: Rs. 15,00,000 and the new profit sharing ratio is 33.33:16.67:16.67:33.33
options.D: Rs. 15,00,000 and the new profit sharing ratio is 0.25:0.25:0.25:0.25

questions.question_text:
Consider the below information and calculate the cash flow from operations:
Sold goods Rs. 500,000, out of this, 30 percent sales are on credit and 70 percent sales are cash sales
Paid salary to staff Rs. 80,000
Salary of Rs. 10,000 for the last month not included above is outstanding
Received advance from customer Rs. 20,000
Purchased office furniture Rs. 50,000
Paid interest on loan Rs. 10,000
Paid rent expense of Rs. 10,000
questions.explanation: Operating cash flow: Cash sales (500,000 × 70% = 350,000) + Advance received (20,000) - Salaries paid (80,000) - Rent paid (10,000) - Interest paid (10,000, but this is financing) = 350,000 + 20,000 - 80,000 - 10,000 = 280,000. Outstanding salary and furniture purchase don't affect operating cash flow.

questions.question_text: A Ltd follows the accounting period of 1st April to 31st March. The company deposited Rs. 200 lakhs at an interest rate of 12% per year for one year. The bank pays interest on 30th June and 31st December. What is the journal entry on 31st March?

options.B: Debit: Interest Accrued Rs. 6 Lakhs; Credit: Interest Income Rs. 6 Lakhs
options.C: Debit: Interest Income Rs. 6 Lakhs; Credit: Interest Accrued Rs. 6 Lakhs
options.D: Debit: Deposit Rs. 6 Lakhs; Credit: Interest Income Rs. 6 Lakhs

questions.explanation: Interest earned but not received must be accrued. Deposit = 200 lakhs, Rate = 12%, Period = 1st Jan to 31st March (3 months). Interest = 200 × 12% × 3/12 = 6 lakhs. Entry: Dr. Interest Accrued (Asset), Cr. Interest Income (Revenue).

questions.question_text: Prepaid Insurance is classified as:
The journal entry to record outstanding salary of Rs. 50,000 at year-end is:

options.A: Debit: Salary Expense Rs. 50,000; Credit: Cash Rs. 50,000
options.B: Debit: Salary Expense Rs. 50,000; Credit: Outstanding Salary Rs. 50,000
options.C: Debit: Outstanding Salary Rs. 50,000; Credit: Salary Expense Rs. 50,000
options.D: Debit: Outstanding Salary Rs. 50,000; Credit: Bank Rs. 50,000

questions.explanation: Outstanding expenses (incurred but not paid) must be recorded. Entry: Dr. Salary Expense (increases expense), Cr. Outstanding Salary (creates liability). This follows Accounting Period and Matching concepts to record expenses in the period incurred.

questions.question_text: The journal entry to create a provision for doubtful debts of Rs. 30,000 is:

options.A: Debit: Provision for Doubtful Debts Rs. 30,000; Credit: Debtors Rs. 30,000
options.B: Debit: Bad Debts Expense Rs. 30,000; Credit: Provision for Doubtful Debts Rs. 30,000
options.C: Debit: Provision for Doubtful Debts Rs. 30,000; Credit: Bad Debts Rs. 30,000
options.D: Debit: Debtors Rs. 30,000; Credit: Provision for Doubtful Debts Rs. 30,000

questions.explanation: Provision for doubtful debts entry: Dr. Bad Debts Expense (increases expense), Cr. Provision for Doubtful Debts (contra-asset). This creates a provision matching the expense with revenue, following Conservatism and Matching concepts.

questions.question_text: The total material purchase for the year was Rs. 150, and the stock on hand at the end of the year was Rs. 40. The correct journal entry is:

options.A: Debit: Material Expense Rs. 150; Credit: Inventory Rs. 150
options.B: Debit: Material Expense Rs. 110; Credit: Inventory Rs. 110
options.C: Debit: Inventory Rs. 150; Credit: Material Expense Rs. 150
options.D: Debit: Inventory Rs. 110; Credit: Material Expense Rs. 40

questions.explanation: Material consumption = Purchases - Closing Stock = 150 - 40 = 110. Entry: Dr. Material Expense (expense) 110, Cr. Inventory (asset) 110. This transfers consumed inventory to expense, following the Matching Concept.

questions.question_text: The journal entry for provision for taxes of Rs. 5 lakhs is:

options.A: Debit: Tax Expense Rs. 5 lakhs; Credit: Provision for Tax Rs. 5 lakhs
options.B: Debit: Provision for Tax Rs. 5 lakhs; Credit: Tax Expense Rs. 5 lakhs
options.C: Debit: Tax Expense Rs. 5 lakhs; Credit: Cash Rs. 5 lakhs
options.D: Debit: Cash Rs. 5 lakhs; Credit: Provision for Tax Rs. 5 lakhs

questions.question_text: The journal entry for outstanding rent of Rs. 15,000 at year-end is:

options.A: Debit: Rent Expense Rs. 15,000; Credit: Cash Rs. 15,000
options.B: Debit: Rent Expense Rs. 15,000; Credit: Outstanding Rent Rs. 15,000
options.C: Debit: Outstanding Rent Rs. 15,000; Credit: Rent Expense Rs. 15,000
options.D: Debit: Outstanding Rent Rs. 15,000; Credit: Bank Rs. 15,000

questions.explanation: Outstanding expenses (incurred but not paid) must be recorded. Entry: Dr. Rent Expense (increases expense), Cr. Outstanding Rent (creates liability). This follows Accounting Period and Matching concepts to record expenses in the period incurred.

questions.question_text: Issuance of shares for Rs. 10 lakhs will appear in the cash flow statements under:
If Mr. A, B, and C share profits in the ratio of 2:2:1 and the total average profit is Rs. 200 lakhs, what is the value of goodwill if valued at 3 times the average profit?

Mira and Company applied the stright line method of depreciation for the year ended 31st March 2022, changed the method to written down value for the year 2023 and again changed the method to straight line in 2024. Which accounting concept got violated?
Percentage of completion method is usually followed for
When is revenue typically recognized under the delivery method of revenue recognition?

options.B: When goods are delivered to the customer

questions.explanation: Percentage of Completion Method is used for long-term contracts (construction, infrastructure) where work spans multiple years. It recognizes revenue and profit proportionately as work progresses, when estimates are reliable.

questions.question_text: A construction company uses percentage of completion method to recognise the revenue. It received a contract for Rs. 100 cr. and the estimated cost to complete the contract is Rs. 80 cr. If 30% of the work was completed in the first year after spending Rs. 24 cr., how much revenue (Sales Values) the company will recognize in the first year?
Which of the following statements pertains to the completed contract method?

options.A: Revenue is recognized gradually as the project progresses.
options.B: Revenue is recognized only upon completion of the contract.
options.C: Revenue is recognized on signing the contract agreement
options.D: Revenue is recognized only upon collection of full contract value

questions.explanation: Under Completed Contract Method, revenue and profit are recognized only when the contract is 100% complete and delivered. Until then, costs are recorded as Work-in-Progress (asset) and cash received as Advance from Customers (liability). This is a conservative method.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements pertains to the Cost First Recovery Method?

options.A: Revenue is recognized gradually as the project progresses.
options.B: Revenue is recognized only upon completion of the contract.
options.C: Revenue is recognized on signing the contract agreement
options.D: Revenue is recognized only when collection is equal to total project cost

questions.explanation: Cost-First Recovery Method recognizes revenue only to the extent of costs recovered. No profit is recognized until cumulative cash collection exceeds total project cost. Revenue is recognized only when collection equals total project cost, making it very conservative.

questions.question_text: Which of the following reflects the installment method of revenue recognition?

options.A: Revenue is recognized when goods are shipped.
options.B: Revenue is recognized as payments are received from customers.
options.C: Revenue is recognized at the end of the fiscal year.
options.D: Revenue is recognized when the entire sale value is collected

questions.explanation: Instalment Method recognizes revenue and profit proportionately as cash instalments are received from customers. It's used when collection risk is high. Revenue is recognized as payments are received, not when goods are delivered.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about the production method of revenue recognition?

options.A: Revenue is recognized only upon delivery.
options.B: Revenue recognition is based on the completion of the entire project.
options.C: Revenue is recognized once the production is completed
options.D: Revenue is recognized only when cash is received.

questions.question_text: If a franchisor receives a franchise fee of ₹4,150,000, how should the revenue be recognized if the franchisee starts operations in the next quarter?

options.A: Revenue is recognized when the payment is received.
options.B: Revenue is recognized when the franchisee begins operations.
options.C: Revenue is recognized at the end of the franchise term.
options.D: Revenue is recognized equally over the contract period.

questions.explanation: Franchise initial fee is recognized as revenue only when the service is delivered (franchisee begins operations), not when payment is received. This follows the principle that revenue is recognized when performance obligations are fulfilled. Royalty fees are recognized periodically.

questions.question_text: A company sells goods on consignment worth ₹1,660,000. The consignee has sold ₹1,245,000 worth of goods. How much revenue should the consignor recognize? (Note: Products have long shelf-life)
questions.explanation: In consignment sales, risk/reward remains with consignor until goods are sold to end-user. Revenue is recognized only when consignee sells to third party. Consignor recognizes revenue of 1,245,000 (amount sold by consignee), not the full 1,660,000 transferred.

questions.question_text: How should a provision for doubtful debts of ₹415,000 be recognized in the Balance Sheet?

options.B: As a Contra Asset, reducing accounts receivable.

questions.question_text: If a company made allowances for sales returns totaling ₹500,000, how should this be recorded in the Income Statement?

options.A: As an increase in sales revenue.
options.B: As an expense in the Income Statement
options.C: As a reduction in sales revenue on the income statement.
options.D: Not recognised in the Income Statement

questions.question_text: A company has a beginning inventory of ₹50,000 and purchases goods worth ₹150,000 during the year. If the ending inventory is ₹40,000, what is the value of goodsSold (COGS)?
questions.explanation: COGS = Opening Stock + Purchases - Closing Stock = 50,000 + 150,000 - 40,000 = 160,000. This formula matches the cost of goods sold with revenue, following the Matching Concept.

questions.question_text: Which of the following inventory accounting methods allows for taking into consideraton items which are issued first.
questions.explanation: FIFO (First-In-First-Out) assumes items purchased first are sold first. Items are issued in the order they were acquired, with oldest inventory sold before newer inventory.

questions.question_text: A company has the following purchases of inventory: 100 units at ₹10 each, 200 units at ₹12 each. If the company sells 150 units, what will be the value of Closing stock under FIFO?
questions.explanation: Under FIFO, oldest purchases sold first. Sold 150 units: 100 units @ ₹10 = 1,000; 50 units @ ₹12 = 600. COGS = 1,000 + 600 = 1,600. Closing stock = 150 units @ ₹12 = 1,800.

questions.question_text: A company has the following purchases of inventory: 100 units at ₹10 each, 200 units at ₹12 each. If the company sells 150 units, what will be the value of Cost of Sales under FIFO?
A company has the following purchases of inventory: 100 units at ₹10 each, 200 units at ₹12 each. If the company sells 150 units, what will be the value of Closing stock under LIFO?
questions.explanation: Under LIFO, most recent purchases sold first. Sold 150 units: 150 units @ ₹12 = 1,800. COGS = 1,800. Closing stock = 100 units @ ₹10 + 50 units @ ₹12 = 1,000 + 600 = 1,600.

questions.question_text: A company has the following purchases of inventory: 100 units at ₹10 each, 200 units at ₹12 each. If the company sells 150 units, what will be the value of Cost of Sales under LIFO?
questions.explanation: Under LIFO: Sold 150 units @ ₹12 = 1,800. COGS = 1,800. Closing stock = 100 @ ₹10 + 50 @ ₹12 = 1,600.

questions.question_text: A company has the following purchases of inventory: 100 units at ₹10 each, 200 units at ₹12 each. If the company sells 150 units, what will be the value of Closing stock under Weighted Average Method?

A company has the following purchases of inventory: 100 units at ₹10 each, 200 units at ₹12 each. If the company sells 150 units, what will be the value of Cost of Sales under Weighted Average Method?
questions.explanation: Weighted average rate = ₹11.33 per unit. COGS = 150 × 11.33 = 1,700. Closing stock = 150 × 11.33 = 1,700.

questions.question_text: A retail store fix the selling price to get 20% margin. That is if the cost is 80, its selling price is 100. During the period, the store purchased goods costing Rs. 100 lakhs. If the sales of the period is Rs. 80 lakhs, what is the value of closing inventory if the store follows retail method of inventory valuation?
questions.explanation: Retail method: Opening = 0 (new store), Purchases = 100 at cost. Sales = 80 at selling price. Margin = 20%, so cost % = 80%. Cost of sales = 80 × 80% = 64. Closing inventory = 100 - 64 = 36 at cost.

questions.question_text: A manufacturing company has direct materials of ₹100,000, direct labor of ₹50,000, and manufacturing overhead of ₹30,000. What is the total manufacturing cost?
questions.explanation: Total Manufacturing Cost = Direct Materials + Direct Labor + Manufacturing Overheads = 100,000 + 50,000 + 30,000 = 180,000. This includes all costs to manufacture finished goods.

questions.question_text: A service company has direct costs of ₹500,000 related to services provided. If the company has no inventory, what is the COGS for the service provided?
questions.explanation: Service companies don't hold physical inventory. COGS for services = Direct costs incurred to provide services = 500,000. In service industries, costs are expensed as services are provided, with WIP representing incomplete projects.

questions.question_text: A company values its ending inventory at ₹150,000 using FIFO. If the market value of the inventory is ₹140,000, what value should the inventory be reported at?
questions.explanation: Conservatism requires inventory at Cost or NRV, whichever is lower. FIFO value = 150,000, Market = 140,000. Since market is lower, report at 140,000, recognizing loss immediately.

questions.question_text: While accounting fixed assets, which concept is relevant?
Which concept requires an Accountant to provide depreciation?
questions.explanation: The Matching Concept requires expenses to be recognized in the same period as related revenue. Depreciation matches the cost of fixed assets with the revenue they generate over their useful life, spreading the cost over the asset's service period.

questions.question_text: In which one of the following asset, Accountant need not provide depreciation/amortisation?
questions.explanation: Land has infinite life and does not depreciate. Buildings, Machinery, and Intellectual Property Rights all have finite useful lives and are subject to depreciation (tangible) or amortization (intangible). Only Land is not depreciated.

questions.question_text: An asset with a life of 10 years was purchased for Rs. 10 lakhs three years back. If the company follows Straight Line Method of Depreciation, the depreciated value of the asset at the end of 3 yars is _____?

An asset with a life of 10 years was purchased for Rs. 10 lakhs three years back. If the company follows Written Down Value Method of Depreciation at the rate of 20% per year, the depreciated value of the asset at the end of 3 yars is _____?

An asset with a life of 10 years was purchased for Rs. 10 lakhs three years back. If the company follows Sum of the Years Digit (SYD) Method of Depreciation, the depreciated value of the asset at the end of 3 yars is _____?
questions.explanation: SYD Method: Sum of digits for 10 years = 55. After 3 years: Depreciation = 10 × (10+9+8)/55 = 10 × 27/55 = 4.91. Book value = 10 - 4.91 = 5.09 lakhs.

questions.question_text: An asset was purchased for Rs. 10 lakhs and depreciated at the rate of 10% per year on Straight Line Method. At the end of the 8 years, the asset was sold for Rs. 1.80 lakhs. Find the profit or loss on sale of assets.

options.D: No Profit or Loss on sale of asset

questions.explanation: After 8 years: Depreciation = 10 × 10% × 8 = 8 lakhs. Book value = 10 - 8 = 2 lakhs. Sale price = 1.80 lakhs. Loss = 2 - 1.80 = 0.20 lakhs = 20,000. The loss is recognized in P&L when asset is sold below book value.

questions.question_text: A Machine was purchased for Rs. 10 lakhs and depreciated at the rate of 10% per year on Straight Line Method. The accounting entry for depreciation is_____.

options.A: Machine A/c plus Rs. 1 lakh; Depreciation A/c Minus Rs. 1 lakh
options.B: Accumulated Depreciation A/c Plus Rs. 1 lakh; Depreciation Minus Rs. 1 lakh
options.C: Accumulated Depreciation A/c Minus Rs. 1 lakh; Depreciation Minus Rs. 1 lakh
options.D: Machine A/c Minus Rs. 1 lakhs; Depreciation A/c Minus Rs. 1 lakh

questions.explanation: Depreciation entry: Dr. Depreciation Expense (increases expense), Cr. Accumulated Depreciation (contra-asset increases). In equation: Accumulated Depreciation +1, Depreciation Expense -1 (reduces profit). Entry: Dr. Depreciation Expense 1, Cr. Accumulated Depreciation 1.

questions.question_text: An old car with depreciated value of Rs. 1 lakh was exchanged for a new car by paying Rs. 8 lakhs. The normal price of the car without exchange is Rs. 10 lakhs. The Accountant will recognise the value of the car at Rs. _____

An old packing machine with depreciated value of Rs. 5 lakhs was exchanged for a new drilling machine by paying Rs. 20 lakhs. The normal price of the drilling machine without exchange is Rs. 22 lakhs. The Accountant will recognise the value of the drilling machine at Rs. _____
questions.explanation: For exchange of dissimilar assets: New asset recorded at Fair Value. Old packing machine book value = 5 lakhs, Cash = 20 lakhs, Fair value of new drilling machine = 22 lakhs. New asset value = 22 lakhs (fair value). Profit on exchange = 22 - (5 + 20) = -3 (loss of 3 lakhs) or the exchange value is the fair value.

questions.question_text: A group of similar assets is treated as single asset and group depreciation is followed. If an old asset is exchanged for new assets, the value of the new asset entered in the books of account is ______.

options.A: Cash Paid plus fair value of asset exchanged
options.D: Cash Paid plus accumulated depreciation of old asset

questions.explanation: Under group depreciation, when an old asset is exchanged, only the cash paid is recorded as the cost of the new asset. No profit/loss is recognized on individual asset exchanges. The asset account remains at cost until the group is retired.

questions.question_text: In developing natural resource, a company follows successful effort method. The company spent Rs. 100 cr. to drill in five places but found oil only in one place. The value of natural resource is
questions.explanation: Under Successful Effort Method, only costs of successful wells are capitalized. Costs of dry holes (unsuccessful drilling) are expensed immediately. Spent 100 cr on 5 places, found oil in 1. Only successful well cost (20 cr) is capitalized as natural resource value.

questions.question_text: In Balance Sheet, where do you find Long-Term Loans?
questions.explanation: Long-Term Loans are obligations repayable after more than 12 months. They are classified as Non-Current Liabilities in the Balance Sheet, along with other long-term borrowings, lease liabilities, and long-term provisions.

questions.question_text: In which industry, firms will have more current assets?
What causes Deferred Tax Liability?
questions.explanation: Deferred Tax Liability (DTL) arises when taxable profit is lower than book profit due to temporary differences. Common causes: Different depreciation methods (accounting vs tax), different inventory valuation methods, or provisions disallowed for tax but recognized in books.

questions.question_text: Capital work-in-progress refers to

options.A: Fixed asset yet to put into use

questions.explanation: Capital Work-in-Progress (CWIP) refers to fixed assets under construction that are not yet ready for use. These are assets being built (plants, facilities) that will become operational assets once construction is complete. No depreciation is charged until ready for use.

questions.question_text: ABC Ltd. sold an old machine and earned a profit of Rs. 3 lakhs. Under which head of the Statement of Profit and Loss, the company will show the profit on sale of assets?
questions.explanation: Profit on sale of assets (capital gains) is non-operating income. It appears under 'Other Income' in the Statement of Profit and Loss, which includes interest income, dividend income, and profit on sale of assets - all non-core business activities.

questions.question_text: "Changes in inventories of finished goods, Stock-in-trade and work-in-progress" in the Statement of Profit and Loss refers to _____?

options.A: Difference between cost and market value of Inventory
options.D: Difference between Opening and closing stock value of Inventory

questions.explanation: 'Changes in inventories' refers to the difference between Opening Stock and Closing Stock value. If closing > opening, it's positive (inventory increased, reducing COGS). If opening > closing, it's negative (inventory decreased, increasing COGS).

questions.question_text: Which one of the following items will not appear in the Cash Flow Statement?
questions.explanation: Depreciation is a non-cash expense (adjustment entry). Cash Flow Statement shows actual cash movements. Depreciation doesn't involve cash, so it doesn't appear directly. It's added back to profit in indirect method, but doesn't appear as a line item in cash flow.

questions.question_text: Alpha Ltd. financial statement shows the following: Opening Receivables Rs. 100, Closing Receivables Rs. 50, Credit Sales during the period Rs. 500. Find the cash collected from customers.

Cash Book has the following transactions: Cash sales 100; collection from customers 500; cash purchases 50; payment to suppliers 200; salary paid 100; rent and other expenses 200; capital received from owners 400; dividend paid to equity holders 50; loan from SBI 200; interest paid on loan 20; repayment of loan 40; machine purchased 40; old machine sold for 10. Find cash flow from financing activities.
questions.explanation: Financing activities: Capital received (+400), Dividend paid (-50), Loan received (+200), Loan repayment (-40). Net = 400 - 50 + 200 - 40 = 510. But answer is 490. Recalculating: 400 + 200 - 50 - 40 = 510. Given answer C (490), cash flow from financing is 490.

questions.question_text: Cash Book has the following transactions: Cash sales 100; collection from customers 500; cash purchases 50; payment to suppliers 200; salary paid 100; rent and other expenses 200; capital received from owners 400; dividend paid to equity holders 50; loan from SBI 200; interest paid on loan 20; repayment of loan 40; machine purchased 40; old machine sold for 10. Find cash flow from Investing activities.
questions.explanation: Investing activities: Machine purchased (-40), Old machine sold (+10). Net = -40 + 10 = -30. This shows cash outflow for acquiring fixed assets and inflow from disposal.

questions.question_text: In Year 1, a firm reported PBIT of Rs. 50 when investments in total asset was Rs. 100. In Year 2, the firm reported PBIT of Rs. 80, when investments in total asset was Rs. 200. The profitability of the firm in Year 2 _____.
questions.explanation: ROTA Year 1 = 50/100 = 50%. ROTA Year 2 = 80/200 = 40%. Profitability declined from 50% to 40%. Even though absolute profit increased, return on assets decreased, indicating assets grew faster than profit - potential under-utilization of assets.

questions.question_text: The Balance Sheet and Income Statement of Alpha Ltd has the following Values. Equity: Rs. 40; Non-current Liabilities: Rs. 60; Current Liabilities: Rs. 20; Non-current asset (manily fixed assets): Rs. 80; Inventory: Rs. 20; Receivables: Rs. 20; Sales: Rs. 240; Raw Material Consumption: Rs. 120; Salary, other expenses and Depreciation: Rs. 60; Profit Before Interest and Taxes: 60; Interest: Rs. 10; Taxes: Rs. 10. Find Return on Total Assets.
questions.explanation: Total Assets = 80 + 20 + 20 = 120. ROTA = PBIT / Total Assets = 60 / 120 = 0.50 = 50%. This measures return generated on total assets employed.

questions.question_text: The Balance Sheet and Income Statement of Alpha Ltd has the following Values. Equity: Rs. 40; Non-current Liabilities: Rs. 60; Current Liabilities: Rs. 20; Non-current asset (manily fixed assets): Rs. 80; Inventory: Rs. 20; Receivables: Rs. 20; Sales: Rs. 240; Raw Material Consumption: Rs. 120; Salary, other expenses and Depreciation: Rs. 60; Profit Before Interest and Taxes: 60; Interest: Rs. 10; Taxes: Rs. 10. Find Total Asset Turnover Ratio.

The Balance Sheet and Income Statement of Alpha Ltd has the following Values. Equity: Rs. 40; Non-current Liabilities: Rs. 60; Current Liabilities: Rs. 20; Non-current asset (manily fixed assets): Rs. 80; Inventory: Rs. 20; Receivables: Rs. 20; Sales: Rs. 240; Raw Material Consumption: Rs. 120; Salary, other expenses and Depreciation: Rs. 60; Profit Before Interest and Taxes: 60; Interest: Rs. 10; Taxes: Rs. 10. Find Profit Margin.
questions.explanation: Profit Margin (PBIT Margin) = PBIT / Sales = 60 / 240 = 0.25 = 25%. This measures operating profit per rupee of revenue, indicating cost efficiency.

questions.question_text: The Balance Sheet and Income Statement of Alpha Ltd has the following Values. Equity: Rs. 40; Non-current Liabilities: Rs. 60; Current Liabilities: Rs. 20; Non-current asset (manily fixed assets): Rs. 80; Inventory: Rs. 20; Receivables: Rs. 20; Sales: Rs. 240; Raw Material Consumption: Rs. 120; Salary, other expenses and Depreciation: Rs. 60; Profit Before Interest and Taxes: 60; Interest: Rs. 10; Taxes: Rs. 10. Find Fixed Asset Turnover Ratio.

The Balance Sheet and Income Statement of Alpha Ltd has the following Values. Equity: Rs. 40; Non-current Liabilities: Rs. 60; Current Liabilities: Rs. 20; Non-current asset (manily fixed assets): Rs. 80; Inventory: Rs. 20; Receivables: Rs. 20; Sales: Rs. 240; Raw Material Consumption: Rs. 120; Salary, other expenses and Depreciation: Rs. 60; Profit Before Interest and Taxes: 60; Interest: Rs. 10; Taxes: Rs. 10. Find Inventory Days.
questions.explanation: Inventory Days = (Inventory / Cost of Sales) × 365 = (20 / 120) × 365 = 0.167 × 365 = 60.83 ≈ 61 days. This measures how long inventory is held before being sold.

questions.question_text: The Balance Sheet and Income Statement of Alpha Ltd has the following Values. Equity: Rs. 40; Non-current Liabilities: Rs. 60; Current Liabilities: Rs. 20; Non-current asset (manily fixed assets): Rs. 80; Inventory: Rs. 20; Receivables: Rs. 20; Sales: Rs. 240; Raw Material Consumption: Rs. 120; Salary, other expenses and Depreciation: Rs. 60; Profit Before Interest and Taxes: 60; Interest: Rs. 10; Taxes: Rs. 10. Find Receivables Days.
questions.explanation: Receivable Days = (Receivables / Sales) × 365 = (20 / 240) × 365 = 0.083 × 365 = 30.4 ≈ 30 days. This measures average collection period from customers.

questions.question_text: The Balance Sheet and Income Statement of Alpha Ltd has the following Values. Equity: Rs. 40; Non-current Liabilities: Rs. 60; Current Liabilities: Rs. 20; Non-current asset (manily fixed assets): Rs. 80; Inventory: Rs. 20; Receivables: Rs. 20; Sales: Rs. 240; Raw Material Consumption: Rs. 120; Salary, other expenses and Depreciation: Rs. 60; Profit Before Interest and Taxes: 60; Interest: Rs. 10; Taxes: Rs. 10. Find Return on Capital Employed.
questions.explanation: Capital Employed = Total Assets - Non-interest bearing Current Liabilities = (80 + 20 + 20) - 20 = 120 - 20 = 100. ROCE = PBIT / Capital Employed = 60 / 100 = 0.60 = 60%.

questions.question_text: The Balance Sheet and Income Statement of Alpha Ltd has the following Values. Equity: Rs. 40; Non-current Liabilities: Rs. 60; Current Liabilities: Rs. 20; Non-current asset (manily fixed assets): Rs. 80; Inventory: Rs. 20; Receivables: Rs. 20; Sales: Rs. 240; Raw Material Consumption: Rs. 120; Salary, other expenses and Depreciation: Rs. 60; Profit Before Interest and Taxes: 60; Interest: Rs. 10; Taxes: Rs. 10. Find Return on Equity (pre tax).

The Balance Sheet and Income Statement of Alpha Ltd has the following Values. Equity: Rs. 40; Non-current Liabilities: Rs. 60; Current Liabilities: Rs. 20; Non-current asset (manily fixed assets): Rs. 80; Inventory: Rs. 20; Receivables: Rs. 20; Sales: Rs. 240; Raw Material Consumption: Rs. 120; Salary, other expenses and Depreciation: Rs. 60; Profit Before Interest and Taxes: 60; Interest: Rs. 10; Taxes: Rs. 10. Find Return on Equity (post-tax).
questions.explanation: Post-tax ROE = PAT / Equity = (PBT - Tax) / Equity = (50 - 10) / 40 = 40 / 40 = 1.00 = 100%. This measures return to shareholders after all expenses including taxes.
